headline: Shaberu has no known origin, but is listed in the Nippo Jisho of 1603, with an earliest appearance possibly in the early 1300s.
Kozeni is 小 (ko-, “little”) plus 銭 (zeni, “coins; money”).
Arayuru is a fossilized passive of ar-, “to be, to exist”, one of the few expressions that kept the old passive marker.
Hantai is from Sinitic 反對.
Horu, “to carve”, is a doublet of 掘る (horu, “to dig”), and went poru > ɸoru > horu.
Kutōten is 句読 (kutō) plus 点 (ten).
Sō ieba is そう (sō, “like that, so”) plus 言えば (ieba), literally “speaking of that....”.
Shokugyō is, by surface analysis, 職 (shoku) plus 業 (-gyō).
Oshare is 御 (o-, honorific prefix) plus 洒落 (share).
Min'yō is a calque of German Volkslied.
Ossharu is an alteration of おおせある (ōse aru).
Kona appears to be 粉 (ko, “powder”) plus an unclear suffix な (-na), first cited to 1683.
Hā is onomatopoeic.
Rōjin is compared with Proto-Ryukyuan *oe-pito, which uses native elements.
Nakayubi is 中 (naka, chū, “middle”) plus 指 (yubi, shi, “finger”).
Misu is from English mistake or miss, and a separate entry covers English Miss.
Hyōshiki is Middle Chinese 標識.
Ikenai is the negative of 行ける (ikeru), the potential form of 行く (iku).
Ishi was coined by Nishi Amane as a translation of English will, and became established through the Tetsugaku Jii of Inoue Tetsujirō.
Betsu ni is 別 (betsu, “separate”) plus に (ni): literally separately, used idiomatically to mean especially; compare Korean 별로 (byeollo).
Yōmō is 羊 (yō, “sheep”) plus 毛 (mō, “hair”).
Keredo is a clipping of けれども (keredomo, “although, but”), first attested in 1711.
Saru's ultimate derivation is possibly borrowed from Ainu サロ (saro, “monkey”).
Takamaru is 高 (taka, root of 高い, “high, tall”) plus -maru, developed from Classical Japanese 高む.
Sayū is 左 (sa, “left”) plus 右 (yū, “right”).
Uketoru is 受ける (ukeru, “to receive”) plus 取る (toru, “to take”).
Nezumi was originally 根 (ne, “root”, signifying somewhere hidden away) plus 住み (sumi, “to live”): “one who lives in hidden places”.
Kuu went from kupu through kuwu to kuu; the medial w vanishes but resurfaces in kuwanai and kuwareru.
Joō is Middle Chinese 女王, literally “female + king”.
Jōkyō is Middle Chinese 上 (MC dzyangX) plus 京 (MC kjaeng).
Minoru is usually considered 実 (mi, “fruit”) plus 乗る (noru, “to ride”), though noru may be a corruption of なる (naru, “to bear fruit”).
